rv.q: This harrowing, tough-minded musical about mental illness, trauma, love and family is a genuinely courageous attempt to expand the form.
Where this show unambiguously succeeds is in its sympathetic but clear-sighted depiction of a family buckling under buried grief and an impossible present.

It’s a great idea for a musical: a suburban mum battles her bipolar disorder in the discomfort of her own home. Great enough, indeed, that before Tom Kitt and Brian Yorkey’s show made its British debut last autumn at the Donmar Warehouse, it was a Broadway hit in 2009 and won a Pulitzer prize for drama in 2010.
The cast's energy and talent is showcased and driven by an accomplished modern score, delivered by a 6-piece band who occupy 3 distinct panels above the main playing area.
It remains a landmark piece of musical theatre, combining raw emotion with musical excellence.
Kitt and Yorkey’s musical soars in the hands of such an accomplished and connected cast.

If not already obvious, every performer on stage gives a strong performance. With a cult following and complex subject matter, it's a difficult musical to bring to the stage, but they do it with grace and ease, aided by direction from Michael Longhurst. Next to Normal is not quite a perfect musical; its subplot with Natalie going off the rails lacks edge and the big conclusion is a little too neat, but there is power in moments and a greatness in its overall effect that still makes this 16-year-old musical a revelation.
Equal parts heartbreaking and heart-wrenching, Next to Normal is the kind of show that you're left thinking about long after you've left the theatre.
It is a genius performance that carries the show, burning a mark of unsettledness into our brains, with many unanswered questions hovering into the night and wounds left gaping wide open.
The blend of humour and gravity is perfectly balanced as the cast bursts onto stage through the kitchen fridge sporting big grins and white medical coats.

The musical, bold in conception, skilled in execution
The creative elements here are impossible to enthuse about: lightweight characters, flimsy music, forgettable costumes.
This is an emotional roller coaster on an epic scale that is not to be missed.

The subject matter is of course not for everyone, and some are sure to be triggered, but with one in four of us experiencing some form of mental health problem every year, it is only right that such a production is afforded a platform of this scale. cn.t: Critics praise this emotionally powerful musical about mental illness for its raw subject matter and strong performances, particularly Caissie Levy's, though some find the material lightweight and its treatment of mental health less specific than needed.
